It's also the first appearance of the weak/strong distinction that §4.1 turns into a full hierarchy — the weak law is convergence in probability, the strong law is convergence almost surely, and the CLT gives only convergence in distribution.
r.math: Chebyshev on μ̂<sub>n</sub>: P(|μ̂<sub>n</sub>−μ| ≥ ε) ≤ Var(μ̂<sub>n</sub>)/ε² = σ²/(nε²). Needs finite σ².

cards.q: Derive the binomial distribution from repeated Bernoulli trials. Give its p.m.f., mean, and variance.
cards.a:
Repeat a dichotomous experiment: X₁,…,Xn a sample of X ~ Bernoulli(p). The number of successes Y = X₁ + … + Xn is binomial, Y ~ Binomial(n,p), with support {0,1,…,n}.

Proposition 1.9.10.

gY(m) = P(Y = m) = C(n,m) pm(1−p)n−m

E[Y] = nE[X] = np    Var(Y) = n Var(X) = np(1−p)
Where each piece comes from. Independence makes the joint p.m.f. a product, and {Y = m} is the disjoint union over all x with ∑xi = m — every such term equals pm(1−p)n−m, and there are C(n,m) of them. The mean is pure linearity. The variance needs the additivity of variance (Cor 1.8.18) plus mutual independence, so the covariances vanish.

Sanity check. Summing the p.m.f. and applying the binomial theorem gives ∑m C(n,m)pm(1−p)n−m = (p + (1−p))n = 1.

r.rot: flip a biased coin n times, count the heads. the count is binomial. the formula has three parts and each one earns its place: pm for the m successes, (1−p)n−m for the failures, and C(n,m) because you don't care which flips were the heads — that's how many orderings give the same count. mean is np (obvious — n trials, p each). variance np(1−p) is biggest at p = ½ and vanishes at p = 0 or 1, which is right: a coin that always lands heads has no randomness left.
r.ex: Example 1.9.11: a coin landing heads 80% of the time, flipped 3 times. P(all heads) = C(3,3)(0.8)³ = 0.512 and P(all tails) = C(3,0)(0.2)³ = 0.008 — a 64-fold difference from a 4-fold bias, because the bias compounds.
r.why: It's the distribution behind every count-of-successes question, and it's the null distribution in the hot-sauce test of §6.1 — T ~ Binomial(30, ½). Note also that the mean needs no independence and the variance does, the same split as for the sample mean.
r.math: Y = ∑X<sub>i</sub>, X<sub>i</sub> ~ Bernoulli(p) i.i.d. P(Y=m) = C(n,m)p<sup>m</sup>(1−p)<sup>n−m</sup>. E[Y] = np, Var(Y) = np(1−p).

cards.q: Generalize to categorical outcomes: give the multinomial distribution, its mean, and its covariance matrix. Why are the off-diagonal entries negative?
cards.a:
Now the outcomes are categories Ω = {1,…,d}. Take X ~ Cat(p) with support {e₁,…,ed} ⊂ Rd, P(X = ej) = pj > 0 and ∑pj = 1. Then Y = ∑j=1n Xj is multinomial, Y ~ mult(n,p):
gY(x) = ( n choose x₁ x₂ … xd ) ∏j=1d pjxj,   xj ∈ N, ∑xj = n
Linearity of expectation and independence give
E[Y] = ∑m E[Xm] = np

Cov(Y) = ∑m Cov(Xm) = n(diag(p) − ppT)

Why the off-diagonals are negative. The counts are constrained to sum to n, so one category getting more forces the others to get less. Categories are negatively correlated by construction — that is exactly the −ppT term.

r.rot: the binomial counts two outcomes; the multinomial counts d of them. same idea, more buckets: probability for each bucket raised to its count, times a multinomial coefficient for the orderings. the mean is np, one entry per category, no surprise. the covariance is the interesting bit — it's negative off the diagonal. that's forced: the counts have to add up to n, so if one bucket fills up the others have to empty. buckets compete.
r.ex: Example 1.9.12, d = 2 with p = (p, 1−p): the multinomial is the binomial, and Σ = np(1−p)[[1,−1],[−1,1]]. The (1,1) entry is n times the Bernoulli variance, and the off-diagonal is the covariance of X with 1−X — same size, opposite sign, because success and failure are perfectly negatively correlated.
r.why: It's the count model behind the categorical cross-entropy of §5.6, and it's what converges to the multivariate normal (Example 2.5.14) just as the binomial converges to the univariate one. The forced negative correlation is also why one-hot encoded features are always linearly dependent unless you drop a column — the identifiability problem of §5.1.3.
r.math: Y ~ mult(n,p). E[Y] = np, Cov(Y) = n(diag(p) − pp<sup>T</sup>), singular because ∑Y<sub>j</sub> = n.

cards.q: Distinguish a random variable from a realization. Define a signal and its likelihood.
cards.a:
Before a die is rolled the outcome is uncertain and is described by a distribution. After, the probabilities have been realized and the outcome is certain. The distinction has names:
X : Ω → R is a random variable, taking x with probability P(X = x).
Once an outcome ω is observed, x = X(ω) is a realization (or draw).
For a sample X₁,…,Xn, each ωi gives a realization xi = X(ωi), and the sequence x₁,…,xn is called a signal.

The likelihood of a signal is the joint probability of its being realized — and because the sample is i.i.d., it factors:

P(X₁=x₁,…,Xn=xn) = ∏j=1n P(X = xj)

Closing the loop. The realized average x̄n = (x₁+…+xn)/n is a single draw from the random variable μ̂n, and the law of large numbers says the probability that any particular x̄n is far from μ becomes very small as n → ∞.

r.rot: keep two things apart. the random variable is the machine — the die, before you roll it, described by a distribution. the realization is the number that came out. a whole list of numbers that came out is a signal. and the likelihood of that signal is: assuming the machine works how you think it does, what were the odds of getting exactly this list? for independent draws it's just the individual probabilities multiplied. that one product is the thing every estimation method in the book maximizes.
r.ex: Example 1.9.13: a weighted coin flipped 5 times, X ~ Bernoulli(p). The signal x = (1,0,1,1,1) has likelihood p·(1−p)·p·p·p = p⁴(1−p). Read as a function of p rather than of x, that is the object you maximize.
r.why: This is the definition MLE is built on — §2.3.3 derives maximum likelihood, and §4.5 makes it the central estimation method. The switch in perspective is the whole trick: the same expression is a probability when you fix p and vary x, and a likelihood when you fix x and vary p.
r.math: Realization x = X(ω). Signal = (x₁,…,x<sub>n</sub>). Likelihood = ∏<sub>j</sub>P(X = x<sub>j</sub>), read as a function of the parameter. x̄<sub>n</sub> is one draw from μ̂<sub>n</sub>.

cards.q: Name four things you can estimate from a sample x₁,…,xₙ, and what makes this legal.
cards.a:
1. Expectations — E[k(X)] ≈ (1/n)Σk(xi), for any k with E[k(X)] finite.
2. Probabilities and p.m.f.s — P(X ∈ A) = E[1A(X)] ≈ (1/n)Σ1A(xi).
3. Marginals — if xi = (yi, zi), just discard the zi; the remaining y's are a draw from the marginal.
4. Quantiles — sort the sample and read them off.

What licenses all of it: the law of large numbers, plus the fact that expectation depends only on the distribution. So you may sample from any convenient random variable sharing the distribution you care about. This is the Monte Carlo method.

r.rot: can't compute the integral? don't. sample a bunch, average, walk away. that's monte carlo and it is genuinely that dumb and that powerful. the marginalization one is the best deal in the chapter — you want the distribution of Y but you sampled (Y,Z) pairs? just delete the Z column. that's marginalization. no integral, no sum, delete the column.
r.ex: Example 1.10.1 — roll a d6, add to your score, reset to 0 on a 6, count rolls to reach 30. Computing E[N] analytically is genuinely painful. Sampling 100,000 games gives 10.45 in a few lines of code.
r.why: Footnote 22 has the trap: the sample mean always exists, even when the expectation it estimates does not. Sample from a Cauchy distribution and you get a number — a meaningless one, because LLN doesn't apply. Your code will not warn you. This is why it ran and gave a number is not evidence of correctness.
r.math: E[k(X)] ≈ (1/n)Σk(x<sub>i</sub>). P(X∈A) ≈ (1/n)Σ1<sub>A</sub>(x<sub>i</sub>). Requires E[k(X)] to exist.

cards.q: In a graphical causal model, what does a missing arrow tell you?
cards.a:
Conditional independence. For any node X in a causal DAG, conditioned on the parents of X, X is conditionally independent of every non-descendant of X.

A missing arrow between two nodes does not mean they are unrelated — it means any relation between them is routed entirely through other nodes in the graph.

The causal reading is interventional: an arrow C → F means forcing C changes F. Forcing F does not change C. That asymmetry is what makes it causal rather than merely correlational. (Ex 1.10.3–1.10.6)

r.rot: the arrows tell you what causes what. the missing arrows are where the actual information is — they tell you what becomes irrelevant once you know the parents. and causation here is defined by force: if i reach in and make C happen, does F move? yes → arrow. if i force F, does C move? no → no arrow back. that asymmetry is the whole definition.
r.ex: Smoking S → yellow nails Y, and S → cancer C, with no arrow between Y and C. Nails and cancer are absolutely correlated. But once you know whether the patient smokes, their nails tell you nothing extra about cancer risk. That's the missing arrow speaking: Y ⊥⊥ C | S.
r.why: This is the yellow-fingernails story from the chapter opener, now made rigorous — treating the symptom does nothing because the arrow runs from the confounder. It's also the structure that makes large probabilistic models tractable, and it sets up the Bayesian networks, HMMs, and graphical models across the rest of Vol 3.
r.math: X ⊥⊥ nondescendants(X) | parents(X). Chain F→S→A gives A ⊥⊥ F | S. Fork Y←S→C gives Y ⊥⊥ C | S.

cards.q: What is the Monte Carlo method, and why is it useful even when you can't write down the p.m.f.?
cards.a:
The law of large numbers says a realization x̄n of the sample mean approximates E[X] closely, with explicit bounds on how far off it is likely to be. Sampling from a distribution — the Monte Carlo method — extends that to almost any property you want.

The key practical point: sampling from a specific random variable may be difficult or expensive, but it is often easy to sample from a different random variable with the same distribution — and the distribution is what you care about.

ȳn = ∑x∈C k(x)gX(x) = E[k(X)] ≈ (1/n)∑i k(xi)
provided E[k(X)] exists (which needs ∑|k(x)|gX(x) < ∞). If E[k(X)²] also exists you get the variance too:
Var(k(X)) ≈ (1/n) ∑i ( k(xi) − ȳn )²

The footnote's warning: the sample mean always exists, even when the expected value it estimates does not. If E[X] doesn't exist, the law of large numbers doesn't apply and the number you computed is meaningless.

r.rot: you want a number about a distribution and the algebra is horrible. so don't do the algebra — simulate. draw a hundred thousand samples and average. that's monte carlo, and it works because the law of large numbers guarantees the average converges. it also works when you have no closed form at all, as long as you can describe the process well enough to run it. the one trap: the sample mean is always computable, even when the thing it's estimating doesn't exist. a number always comes out. that doesn't mean it means anything.
r.ex: Example 1.10.1: roll a die repeatedly adding to your score, but a six resets you to zero — how many rolls to first reach 30? Computing this analytically takes work; Algorithm 1.1 is nine lines of Python. 100,000 runs give a mean of 10.45, and the whole p.m.f. comes out of the same samples as gN(k) ≈ (1/100000)∑1N=k(ni).
r.why: It's the reason generative AI is in this chapter at all — LLMs produce output by sampling from a learned distribution. It's also what makes non-conjugate Bayesian analysis practical (§4.7.1): the intractable posterior integrals are done by Monte Carlo, which is why Bayesian statistics only became usable near the end of the 20th century.
r.math: E[k(X)] ≈ (1/n)∑k(x<sub>i</sub>), valid when E[k(X)] exists. Same samples give probabilities via P(X∈A) = E[1<sub>A</sub>(X)] and quantiles by sorting.

cards.q: What is a graphical causal model, and what does an arrow mean? Give the intervention test.
cards.a:
Modelling usually needs a description of the data generation process — how the random variables affect one another and combine to produce the data. That means identifying causes, not just statistical properties.

A graphical causal model is a graph whose nodes are random variables and whose directed edges encode a potential causal relation: the result of one node can potentially impact every node it points to.

For simplicity the book assumes causal models are directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) — no cycles. Vocabulary: Y is a parent of X if there's an edge Y → X; Z is a descendant of X if there's a path X → … → Z, and then X is an ancestor of Z. Every child is potentially influenced by its parents and by all its ancestors. (Nota Bene 1.10.2: not all causal models are DAGs, but DAGs suffice here.)

The intervention test. Ask what happens if you force an outcome.
Example 1.10.3. Three coins, one two-headed and two fair; draw one at random (C) and flip it (F). The model is C → F. Force C to be the two-headed coin and F must come up heads — the flip changed. Force F to be all heads and nothing happens to which coin you drew. The result of F can tell you about C without causing it.

An arrow does not mean the child is determined by the parent — only that the parent has an impact.

r.rot: draw a box for each variable and an arrow from cause to effect. that's the model. the test for whether an arrow belongs, and which way it points, is intervention: if i reach in and force this variable, does that one change? force the coin to be two-headed and the flips change. force the flips to be all heads and the coin you picked is unaffected. seeing tells you about the cause; doing does not change it. that asymmetry is what an arrow encodes and what plain probability cannot express.
r.ex: The DAG restriction is a real assumption, not just convenience — feedback loops (predator/prey, price/demand) are genuinely cyclic. The book flags this and sets it aside; the acyclic case is where the clean conditional-independence theory lives.
r.why: The intervention framing is what separates §1.10 from everything before it. Chapter 0 posed the question (yellow fingernails predict cancer but bleaching them does nothing); this is the machinery that answers it, and the reason a regression coefficient in §5.3.7 licenses prediction but never intervention.
r.math: DAG: nodes = random variables, directed edges = potential causal influence. Arrow X → Y ⇔ forcing X can change Y. Observation is symmetric; intervention is not.

cards.q: Work through the chain, the fork, and the collider-free chain examples. What does conditioning on a parent buy you in each?
cards.a:
The chain (Example 1.10.4) — fire, smoke, alarm:
F → S → A
Fire causes smoke; smoke causes the alarm. Conditioning on S makes F and A conditionally independent (A ⊥⊥ F | S). Suck away all the smoke, or add extra smoke, and under either intervention the fire has no effect on the alarm and the alarm none on the fire. Conditioning on A gives nothing (A is nobody's parent); conditioning on F gives nothing (everything is a descendant of F, hence exempt).

The fork (Example 1.10.5) — smoking, yellow nails, cancer:

Y ← S → C
The missing arrow Y → C does not mean nails and cancer are unrelated. It means Y ⊥⊥ C | S. Know the patient's smoking habits and looking at his nails tells you nothing more about his cancer risk. Don't know them, and yellow nails inform you about smoking, which informs you about cancer.

The funnel (Example 1.10.6) — two dice A, B, their sum C, and a card total D:

A → C → D  and  B → C
A and B are unconditionally independent (no parents, neither a descendant of the other). D's only parent is C, so D ⊥⊥ A | C and D ⊥⊥ B | C — once you know how many cards to draw, how that number was rolled is irrelevant. And independence is symmetric, so A ⊥⊥ D | C too.

r.rot: three shapes, one lesson. chain F → S → A: the fire only reaches the alarm through the smoke, so once you know the smoke, the fire is irrelevant. fork Y ← S → C: nails and cancer look related because they share a parent; know the parent and the apparent link vanishes. funnel: two dice feed a sum which feeds a card draw — once you know the sum, how it was rolled doesn't matter. in every case, conditioning on the right node cuts the path and the association disappears.
r.ex: The fork is the yellow-fingernails story from Chapter 0 finally drawn as a graph, and the graph explains it in one line: no arrow Y → C, so the entire association was routed through S.
r.why: These three patterns are the vocabulary for reading any causal diagram, and they explain why “controlling for” a variable sometimes removes a spurious association and sometimes destroys a real one — it depends entirely on where the variable sits in the graph. Example 1.10.6 also makes the practical point: the p.m.f. of D would be painful in closed form and is trivial to estimate by sampling the process (Algorithm 1.2).
r.math: Chain X→Z→Y and fork X←Z→Y: conditioning on Z gives X ⊥⊥ Y | Z. Conditioning on a node with no children, or on a common ancestor of everything, adds nothing.
